articles.title: The lonely Chinese men being conned by fake brides
articles.summary: "Flash marriage" scams are an extreme symptom of a demographic crisis long in the making in China.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Chinese man targeted by 'flash wedding' scams By Laura Bicker China correspondent ,  Reporting from Beijing and Guiyang 
- Published 10 August 2026 
At 37, Wang Zhuang had almost given up hope of finding a wife, until he saw the glossy matchmaking adverts. 
They promised he wouldn't have to waste years on building a relationship that had no future. They offered to introduce him to a demure, devoted woman. 
"The matchmakers said that girls from Guizhou are frugal," Wang says. "They told me they are good at running a household, able to do housework, and their families are very poor, so after marrying into your family, they would settle down and live a life with you." 
So Wang travelled to Guiyang, a city in the southwestern province of Guizhou, in the hope of finding his soulmate. 
He thought he had, when he was matched with a woman who seemed to tick every box. They had only met a few times before they married. 
Then, almost as quickly as his new life had begun, it was over. 
"My whole family has been thrown into chaos," he says, shaking his head. 
He is still picking up the pieces more than a year after he discovered that everything he had been told by his wife was a lie. 
She was a former karaoke hostess who'd been married three times, had three children, a serious sexually transmitted disease and was deeply in debt. She had even lied about her age. 
He is fighting for a divorce and cannot return home to his old life - at least until he can recoup some of his life savings, which he says he paid to the agency within hours of being introduced to several potential matches. 
"My parents blame me. I have insomnia and anxiety. I can't focus on work." 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Chinese brides are in huge demand because of a steep gender imbalance 
Wang's story is an extreme symptom of a demographic crisis that has long been in the making in China. 
For decades, China's Communist Party decreed that couples could have only one child. They reversed course in January 2016 but by then the "one-child" policy, coupled with a preference for boys, had produced a shrinking pool of women and a stark gender imbalance. 
There are now 30 million more men than women in China – that's more than the male population of the UK, or the entire population of Australia. 
This has left men like Wang, who are in their late 30s and who live in smaller cities or far-flung, rural areas, with few options. Women in these places can afford to be choosy as they know they are in demand. 
"The requirements for men are very high in my city. You need to have a car, a house and your family should preferably run a business," he says. 
Many families also demand a high "bride price", a longstanding Chinese custom where the groom's family gives money to the bride. In parts of China, where men far outnumber women, this has become a significant financial burden. 
Hence the appeal of matchmaking agencies like the ones in Guizhou, which are proposing a one-stop, quick solution - or "flash marriages". 
Matchmaking agencies are hardly new in China, but many seem to be finding vulnerable targets in men who are struggling to find partners as they grow older. 
So much so that state media recently reported that the industry had seen "rapid growth" which had "bred illegal practices and chaos". 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The "flash marriage" market is now on Beijing's radar 
It's hard to determine the scale of such fraud across China but it has grown enough to draw the attention of Chinese officials. Between January 2024 and March 2025, prosecutors handled cases involving 1,546 individuals for crimes related to the matchmaking industry. 
This month, five separate authorities jointly launched a nationwide crackdown on the matchmaking industry after the issue generated "widespread public concern". 
In one case, a matchmaking agency reportedly used karaoke waitresses as bait to defraud 128 victims of more than 2.5 million yuan (£274,000, $371,000). 
"I think the government could introduce industry-specific regulations targeting flash marriage scams," Fan Binghe, from the Nanjing Office of the Beijing Jingshi law firm, told the BBC. 
Although Guiyang has become synonymous with this booming "flash marriage" market, there is little to suggest it is a romantic hub. 
The agency offices sit in a dense warren of buildings above a shopping precinct, where vendors sell local fruit and workers queue for takeaway sour soup rice noodles. 
Wang, however, was convinced he could trust them after the company told him they would do a full background check and that he would be entitled to compensation if he was the victim of fraud. 
So he paid up and the introductions began. 
Image caption, 
Wang was drawn to Guiyang by the promise of a demure spouse 
He met seven women in various "blind date" rooms over a few days while being carefully supervised by agency staff. He asked questions about where they came from, if they'd been married before and if they had any kids. 
He set his heart on the eighth woman he met. He was hoping to meet someone who hadn't been married before, with no children and who was just a little younger than him. 
"She also dressed very simply," he recalls. "She looked introverted and honest." 
They met four or five times for just eight to 10 minutes each time. He says they had been under strict instructions not to exchange phone numbers or any details on private messages, or they would be fined. 
After two or three days he decided she was the one and he agreed to pay her a substantial bride price. "I spent more than 300,000 yuan [$44,000]," he says, with a pile of well-thumbed legal papers in hand to prove it. 
"If you include the wedding banquet and everything else, I spent around 400,000 to 500,000 yuan." 
The whole process was documented by the matchmaking agency in a series of glossy photos, which they also use to advertise their services on Chinese social media. 
In the video the couple are holding hands on a red carpet and smiling while romantic music plays in the background. 
Image caption, 
Wang with his ex-wife in a photo taken soon after their wedding 
Just months into the marriage, debt collectors started calling, alleging she owed them money. 
Wang grew suspicious and wanted to know what else she had kept hidden. He checked her phone and found details of her former life, her birth certificate and former marriage documents. 
When he confronted her, she offered him a divorce, but refused to return a single penny of the bride price. 
He says he tried to hunt down the agency responsible for his marriage, but when he returned to their offices, they had packed up and disappeared. 
From his rented flat in Guiyang, just across from the main district which houses most of these agencies, Wang now spends his time making social media videos trying to warn other men about what can go wrong. 
In Guiyang, it is difficult to find an agency where the staff is willing to talk. One agency boss agreed to talk to us in their offices – although his business partner later asked us to leave. 
Inside there was a red carpet littered with fake petals ready for a proposal. He told us a couple had pledged to marry just hours before we arrived. 
"There's a huge market for flash marriages in China. It only really emerged over the last two or three years," he told us. 
The agencies claim families here did not strictly adhere to the one-child policy, which means the area has a larger pool of women. "Even if a family had two or three daughters, they would keep trying for a son," one of them told the BBC. 
They say they are now trying to match these women with men from central provinces – like Wang who lives in Hebei – who are relatively wealthy but have few women around them. 
"Our clients are free to choose whoever they like. The purpose of our business is to help people find someone they genuinely want to be with." 
One of the advertisements assures their prospective clients that "Three days with the right introduction can beat three years of dating". 
Image caption, 
It was in a room like this where Wang met his bride 
Wang now spends his time trying to help other victims of similar spiels. 
His rented flat is full of men who are either searching for the owners of the agency who scammed them, or are trying to recoup their losses from their wives who ran off after only a few weeks of marriage. 
On a fold-up bed by the window, 59-year-old Xu Rulin from Jiangxi province pulls his carefully collated evidence out of a red plastic shopping bag. 
He spent nearly 500,000 yuan trying to find his son a wife through a "flash marriage" agency. 
Together they travelled to Guiyang - more than 1,000km away - and his son wed just seven days after he first met his bride in a "blind date" room. 
Xu says after the marriage was registered, she demanded they buy her an iPhone and transfer around 20,000 yuan to help her with her business. She also asked for 120,000 yuan for a wedding dress and jewellery, he claims. 
"All I wanted was for her to genuinely settle down and live with us," he told us. "She said she wanted a house and I agreed to buy one for them. It was all agreed." 
But he says she ran away after living with them for less than two weeks. She has been detained by the police, and the couple have been able to get divorced. 
He says the owners of the matchmaking company were also arrested in January this year, but he is still in Guiyang trying to recover some of the losses. 
Image caption, 
The bride Xu Rulin spent a fortune finding for his son ran away within two weeks 
The agency manager the BBC spoke to admitted there were no formal background checks on their clients. 
"The women are introduced by local matchmakers who already know them very well. They know their family background because they're often from the same village. The male's matchmaker also usually knows the man very well." 
They would not say how much their services cost because that information was "confidential". 
He did say that if the information provided by either side is not truthful, then the client is entitled to get their money back. 
"I'd say more than 90% of what our clients tell us here is true," he claimed. 
"We have a saying here in China. One rotten mouse dropping spoils the whole pot of soup. That's exactly what it's like. We regularly attend meetings with the local police. If a matchmaking agency is found to be involved in marriage fraud, it will be held legally responsible." 
Image caption, 
This matchmaker says most people in the industry are genuine 
This brings little comfort for those who have lost whatever money they had saved. 
"I never imagined that with the agency charging such a high service fee, a local matchmaker in her hometown checking her background and the company offering so many guarantees, that the women's information would turn out to be completely fake," Wang says. 
He is almost resigned now to his losses. And he blames himself for falling for the scam: "Only women with problems would agree to these kind of flash marriages." 
He has kneeled at the police offices in Guiyang pleading for them to help him get his money back and he has even travelled to Beijing to urge the authorities to do more to combat this type of crime. 
These cases are difficult to prosecute, says Fan Binghe, the lawyer who has handled many. 
For one, Chinese law has no specific criminal offence which covers this kind of marriage fraud, and so to bring criminal charges, a victim has to establish that the aim of their spouse was always to take their money. 
"In cases I've handled, suspects often argue that they genuinely intended to marry and live a good life but realised they were incompatible, had conflicts, and decided to end the relationship," he says. 
"In situations like that, the line becomes blurred. Relationship issues are difficult to disprove." 
Image caption, 
Wang's apartment has turned into a refuge for scammed men 
Even harder is getting money back from sham matchmaking agencies which often shut up shop as soon as they have made enough cash. 
Wang has managed to get some money back, but not all. 
"After going through something like this, I don't even know if I can still get married. It was already hard for me to find someone. And now I've spent so much money. I won't consider it now." 
Wang's life, and the life of the men in the apartment, all appear to be in limbo. 
"It has taken almost two years, and even now I still don't know when I can divorce her," he says, surrounded by his legal paperwork. 
"I don't know when this will be resolved, so I can restart a normal life. It feels endless."

articles.title: China evacuates one million from homes as massive storm arrives
articles.summary: Typhoon Dolphin has made landfall, bringing strong winds and heavy rain across eastern China including Shanghai.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Lorry overturns as typhoon hits China By Kelly Ng 
- Published 10 August 2026 
Chinese authorities have evacuated more than a million people from their homes in eastern China including the financial capital Shanghai, as Typhoon Dolphin made landfall. 
The typhoon brought heavy rain and halted transportation across the region. Nearly 1,000 flights were cancelled in Shanghai alone on Monday. 
While authorities have downgraded Dolphin to a tropical storm, they continue to warn of torrential rains, severe flooding and the risk of landslides through to Wednesday as the storm moves north. 
Chinese authorities had earlier issued their highest-level red alert for Dolphin, which is the strongest storm to hit China this year. 
It packed maximum wind speeds of 150km/h (94mph) when it first slammed into Yuhuan in the Zhejiang province at 17:30 (09:30 GMT) on Sunday before making a second landfall in the city of Wenzhou about an hour later, meteorological authorities said. 
Heavy rain was forecast on Monday for the provinces of Shandong, Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and the city of Shanghai. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Typhoon Dolphin made landfall in eastern China on Sunday evening 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Residents wade through flooded streets in Shanghai 
Governments have urged people to avoid outdoor activities, while several top tourist attractions remain closed, including parts of Disneyland and Legoland, and several viewing platforms along the Bund in Shanghai. 
Footage on state media show ground-floor businesses flooded in the former French Concession in Shanghai, an area popular with tourists, and people wading through ankle-deep waters. 
Several state media outlets have reported that a nine-year-old boy from Wenling, Zhejiang is missing after being swept into the sea. Chinese officials have not reported any casualties. 
Parts of Zhejiang could receive 250mm to 500mm of rain over the next few days, forecasters say. 
Authorities in Hangzhou, Zhejiang's capital city, have waived parking fees in all public spaces for drivers seeking shelter amid the strong winds and floodwaters. 
Elsewhere in the province, Wenzhou authorities have relocated some 900,000 residents and opened more than 1,000 emergency shelters, while about 390,000 people have been evacuated from their homes in the city of Taizhou. 
In the coastal province of Fujian, maritime authorities have suspended dozens of passenger ferry routes and halted more than 100 offshore construction projects. 
The storm moved over a long distance of 6,000km before making landfall, suggesting a lifespan of more than three times that of an average typhoon, according to China's state broadcaster CCTV. 
It also has a massive circulation size and intense rainfall capacity, CCTV reported. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
The typhoon has disrupted transportation services 
Misinformation around the storm has apparently spread rapidly on the Chinese internet, with state media reporting that two people have been detained for distributing such content. 
One of them, a 60-year-old man, created a fake video with AI that claimed someone in Shanghai had fallen from a building during the storm. 
Another man, 32, had re-edited storm footage posted by other social media users in a way that was deemed as misleading. 
Dolphin brought torrential rains to the Philippines, parts of northern Taiwan and Japan's Okinawa island before bearing down on China. 
- 
AI or real? BBC analyses viral China disaster videos 
- Published 6 days ago 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
More than 7,000 people are sheltering at evacuation centres nationwide in the Philippines 
Eight people have died in the Philippines because of heavy monsoon rains brought on by Dolphin and storms earlier in the week, says the Office of Civil Defence. More than 7,000 people are sheltering at evacuation centres nationwide. 
In Okinawa in Japan, five elderly people suffered non-life-threatening injuries, according to the prefectural government. 
Three of them fell because of the strong winds, it said. 
Meanwhile in Hong Kong, weather observatory posted a record high temperature of 36.9C on Sunday as the typhoon swept warm air over the city. 
Typhoon season in the western Pacific typically occurs between May and October, when typhoons are considered more commonplace. 
This year is a strong El Niño year, which experts say means typhoons can grow to be more intense.

articles.title: Australia PM under fire for remarks on Japanese counterpart's melon gifts
articles.summary: An ex-Japanese envoy said the "sexist" comments "betrayed the close bond" between the countries.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Australian PM makes controversial “melon” comment on podcast By Kelly Ng   and   Simon Atkinson 
- Published 11 August 2026, 08:55 BST 
Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is under fire for comments he made about two melons gifted to him by his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi, after a former Japanese envoy called it an insult. 
During an appearance on the Bush Deep podcast, Albanese gestured near his chest while referring to the crown melons, calling them "pretty strange" gifts that "ended up being quite good". 
That episode, which aired in July, had already landed the PM in hot water because of "inappropriate" comments he made about popstar Kylie Minogue. 
Opposition leaders are now demanding he apologise to Takaichi, but Albanese's position is that it was the host who made the joke, not him, the BBC understands. 
While discussing the melons Takaichi's team had presented to Albanese during her visit to Australia in May, the host of Bush Deep, comedian Nikki Osborne, quipped: "She brought two... She just came in looking like Pamela Anderson." 
"She brought two, and they are beautiful," Albanese responded. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Japanese prime minister Sanae Takaichi (left) presented Albanese with two royal melons when she visited Australia in May 
The exchange, which drew relatively little interest when the episode aired, has resurfaced after Tokyo's former ambassador to Canberra Shingo Yamagami labelled Albanese's comments a "sexist joke" and said they "betrayed the close bond" between Japan and Australia. 
"The last thing [Takaichi] expected was to be so casually mocked by the trusted leader of Japan's special strategic partner," he wrote in an opinion piece published by The Australian on Monday. 
Crown melons are the "most prized fruit" in Japan and "treasured as something special", Yamagami added, noting that a single melon costs more than 30,000 yen ($188). 
"So, prime minister, please enjoy Japan's sweet and juicy melons without thinking about a woman's anatomy, and instead focus on what our two countries must do together," he said. 
During his two-year stint in Australia, Yamagami had a notably frosty relationship with some members of Albanese's Labor Party over disagreements regarding China. 
An opposition MP asked Albanese on Tuesday if he would apologise for the "foul-mouthed, classless comments about women", to which the prime minister said he "rejected the assertion of the question". 
He went on: "Australia and Japan have never been closer. My government has taken our special strategic partnership to new heights." 
Australia's opposition leader Angus Taylor on Monday also criticised the gaffe as "insulting", and demanded that Albanese make a personal apology. 
Several Labor ministers have jumped to Albanese's defence, saying the former envoy and the media have misinterpreted his comments. 
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said the remarks "were not intended to be interpreted the way that our political opponents and some media outlets are reporting". 
Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek called it "a completely unnecessary interpretation of what the prime minister said". 
"I think people watching it for themselves can make their own minds up," Plibersek told Australia's Channel Seven. 
Plibersek had earlier defended Albanese's controversial remarks about Minogue as nothing more than a sign that he was a fan. 
The prime minister drew a wave of condemnation early last month after Osborne asked him on the podcast whether he would "shag, marry or date" Kylie Minogue, actress Nicole Kidman or entertainer Rhonda Burchmore, to which he replied "Kylie, clearly... all of the above". 
Albanese later issued a public apology, saying: "I apologise unequivocally for the comments". 
Osborne, who is best known for posting crude comedy sketches on YouTube, launched her podcast series earlier this year. Her podcast site describes her as a "wildly inappropriate journalist" who asks "questions no one else would dare".

articles.title: Typhoon Dolphin batters Japan's Okinawa before bearing down on China
articles.summary: The storm has cut power to at least 44,000 buildings and injured five people on the Japanese island.
articles.full_text:
Image source, X/Reuters Image caption, 
The islands of Amami and Okinawa are the parts of Japan most affected by the typhoon By Jack Burgess 
- Published 8 August 2026 
Typhoon Dolphin has cut power to at least 44,000 buildings and injured at least five people after hitting Japan's Okinawa island on Saturday. 
Flights to and from Okinawa's main airport - Naha International Airport - were cancelled as it closed on Friday as the storm arrived. 
The storm had maximum wind speeds of 162km/h (101mph) on Saturday and has been categorised as a "very strong" typhoon by the Japan Meteorological Agency, which warned of high waves, storm surges and lightning strikes. 
Dolphin is expected to make landfall on China's eastern coast late on Sunday or early on Monday. Authorities there have shut ports and schools ahead of its arrival. 
The main areas in Japan affected by the typhoon are the islands of Okinawa and Amami in the far south-west of the country. 
Five elderly people suffered non-life-threatening injuries, according to the Okinawan prefectural government. Three of them fell because of the strong winds, it said. 
Japan's national broadcaster NHK reports numerous accounts of trees being toppled by strong winds throughout Nago city in Okinawa, while a car was found overturned and leaking oil in a parking lot. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Satellite imagery showing Typhoon Dolphin approaching Japan's Okinawa during the week 
In China, Zhejiang's Ningbo Lishe International Airport said it would stop its operations from 23:30 local time on Saturday (15:30 GMT) and suspend all flights on Sunday. 
A coastal typhoon alert in Zhejiang has been raised to its highest level, and port and ferry services have been halted in the Chinese province. 
In Hong Kong, its weather observatory posted a record high temperature of 36.9C on Sunday as Typhoon Dolphin swept warm air over the city. 
Typhoon season in the western Pacific typically occurs between May and October, when typhoons are considered more commonplace. This year is a strong El Niño year , which experts say means typhoons can grow to be more intense. 
In an average year of 25 cyclones reaching tropical storm strength in the region, around three usually make landfall in Japan, according to the country's meteorological agency. 
Some of these will be strong enough to be classified as typhoons – as was the case with Dolphin. 
A typhoon is the term used for storms that form in the north-west Pacific, whereas a hurricane is the term used for storms that form in the Atlantic or eastern Pacific. 
Image source, Japan Meteorological Agency Image caption, 
The typhoon is expected to make landfall on China's eastern coast late on Sunday or early on Monday

articles.title: He's been frozen on Everest for 30 years, now 'Green Boots' may finally be coming home
articles.summary: For decades, an Indian man's lime shoes have been a grim trail marker for many climbing the world's highest peak.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Family handout Image caption, 
Dorje Morup was a keen mountaineer and had climbed many peaks, including Stok Kangri, the highest peak in the Ladakh mountain range By Jehangir Ali BBC News Hindi ,  Reporting from Skurbuchan, Ladakh 
- Published 8 August 2026 
For 30 years, a dead body known as "Green Boots" has been lying in the snow, nestled under an overhanging rock, not far from Mount Everest's summit. 
The lime mountaineering boots worn by an Indian climber who died in 1996 have been a grim trail marker for many climbers on their way up the world's highest peak ever since. 
Now India is looking for a specialist high-altitude recovery team to undertake a complex and risky mission to retrieve what they say is Dorje Morup's body – arguably the most famous of the hundreds whose bodies have been left frozen on the mountain. 
Warning: This story contains a picture of a dead body. 
They hope they are on the cusp of returning his remains to friends and family who never gave up hope he'd come home. 
"On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there'd be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there," Morup's wife told the BBC. 
"When he comes home, I will ask him: 'Where were you all these years?'" 
Disaster struck on descent 
Image source, Supplied Image caption, 
The body of Indian climber Dorje Morup who died 30 years ago wearing his green mountaineering boots has become a grim marker along the road to Everest's summit 
The night before he left to be part of a historic Indian expedition on Everest, Morup sat with his wife at his home in Ladakh, an Indian-administered territory in another part of the Himalayas. 
He made her a promise: that he would come back a hero and make his country proud. 
"He asked me to take care of the kids and come to the airport to greet him on his return," Konchak Yangskit told the BBC at her home. 
A lance naik, or lance corporal, in the Indo Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), the force guarding much of India's border with China, 48-year-old Morup was no stranger to Himalayan trekking. 
But Yangskit says she had a strange sense of foreboding that night: "I wondered if I was ever going to see him again." 
Morup was one of six climbers on the ITBP expedition attempting to reach the top of Everest – which lies on the border between Nepal and the Chinese-governed territory of Tibet. 
Most climbers choose to ascend from the Nepalese side, but Morup's crew wanted to write their names into the history books as the first Indian expedition to do it from the treacherous Chinese side. 
Image caption, 
Morup's wife, Yangskit, says because she never saw his body, she found it difficult to believe he was dead 
Three out of six members of the expedition turned back due to a snowstorm, but Morup and two others - Tsewang Smanla and Tsewang Paljor – kept struggling, all the way up to the 8,849m summit. 
Disaster, a blizzard, struck as they descended and killed all three. 
Like many of the more than 300 people who have died in the Everest region since records began a century ago, their bodies remain on the mountain. 
Two have never been found, but the third body - that of "Green Boots" - has been lying frozen in the snow for three decades at an altitude of 8,500 metres. 
For years, it was assumed that "Green Boots" was another member of the expedition, Tsewang Paljor. 
But testimony from surviving members of the 1996 expedition and the location of the last radio contact with the climbers have now led authorities to believe the remains belong to Morup. 
Image source, Family handout Image caption, 
Morup's family is proud to show the certificate issued by the Chinese government confirming he had successfully reached the top of Everest 
An ITBP official, speaking anonymously because he is not authorised to speak to the media, told BBC News Hindi that Morup's clothes and climbing gear helped officials identify the body in recent years. 
Since then, they've been plotting how to get their comrade home so they can confirm his identity beyond doubt through DNA testing and offer his family a semblance of closure. 
"We never forgot him. It was only a matter of time," the ITBP official said. 
How difficult will it be to recover the body? 
Retrieving those who have died on the mountain is a dangerous, gruelling task, and, up until the past decade, very rare. 
Many of the bodies, like Morup's, are in what climbers call Everest's death zone – where temperatures can plunge to -40C and oxygen levels are about a third of those at sea level. 
"The weather and snow conditions are going to be crucial," said Tshiring Jangbu Sherpa, a prominent Nepalese mountaineer who has taken part in other recovery missions. 
"The north side has fewer crevasses, but it is riskier. If something bad happens from the Nepalese side, you get quickly evacuated by helicopter. But there is no such system from the Chinese side," he told BBC Hindi. 
Image caption, 
Some of photos of Morup and a few of his belongings have helped his family keep his memory alive 
The Chinese side of the peak – where Green Boots' body is – is steeper and doesn't have the same support structures as the southern slope, which is another complicating factor, Sherpa sources have told BBC News Nepali. 
"It's really tough to get that body down even in popular spring season, let alone the autumn [which has more unpredictable weather]. That's the simple reason it is still there for so many years," mountaineering guide Pemba Ongchu Sherpa said. 
"There would need to be 10 to 12 climbers who are capable of making summits, just to fix [support] ropes to reach that point." 
Green Boots will also have to be physically carried down to an altitude where it can be collected by a helicopter, or possibly yaks, and transported back to an airport – a job which also requires huge manpower. 
Sherpas say bodies shrouded in iced-up climbing gear often weigh several times the average man and are frequently frozen into awkward positions, making bringing them down the challenging terrain even more treacherous. The remains may also begin defrosting and decomposing once they reach lower altitudes. 
The start of the descent with the body would be the most difficult, Indian climber Kuntal Joisher told BBC Nepali. 
"It's going to be very, very risky endeavour. It's extremely steep ground with lots of rock. Logistically, this [first] 1000m is going to be a humungous challenge." 
"The main thing is to not put Sherpa lives at risk for a dead body." 
All of this makes for a hugely expensive recovery mission – experts say even the most straightforward ones cost between $40,000 and $80,000, a sum beyond the means of most families. 
It is more common for local teams to move people who have died out of view on the mountain: like explorer Francys Arsentiev, dubbed the Sleeping Beauty of Everest, who in 2007 was moved to a more private final resting place on Everest almost a decade after she died. 
But the ITBP – which is funding the recovery operation – wants Morup's body to be returned by September, and is looking for mountain rescue Sherpa groups who could do the job. 
Once returned to India, the body will undergo DNA testing and, if confirmed to be Morup, his remains will be given back to his family. 
'My heart refused to believe he had died' 
For years, Morup's family back in Ladakh have struggled to come to terms with his disappearance. 
Now around 75, Yangskit struggles to recall even the day she was married. But the days after the tragedy remain etched in her mind. 
"I only knew there was a storm on the mountain. Even though we organised cremation prayers at home, my heart refused to believe he had died," she says with tears rolling down her face. 
"I didn't see his dead body, so it was difficult for me to believe it." 
Image caption, 
Morup's family remains cautious about what the body being returned will mean for them 
Image caption, 
Morup's eldest son, Punchok Dorjai, looks up at a framed photo of his father 
All that remains of Morup today are his medals and trophies, a couple of old photos from his mountain adventures – and, most importantly, a certificate from the Chinese government which states that at 17:30 on 10 May 1996, Morup reached the top of Everest. 
If the recovery mission is successful, Morup's son Punchok Dorjai told the BBC that the family would hold a funeral for him near the Martyrs Park in Ladakh's capital Leh. 
"My father gave his life for the country and he should be remembered as a martyr," Dorjai said, adding that his teammates who perished deserve the same title. 
The family will also proudly save a symbol of Morup's legacy at their home, to go alongside his summit certification, he said: "We are planning to keep the Green Boots." 
Additional reporting by Pradeep Bashyal, BBC News Nepali

articles.title: The transgender controversy surrounding the WNBA
articles.summary: After the Indiana Fever's Sophie Cunningham said it was "common sense" to ban transgender women from women's sports, a row has emerged in the WNBA - with former NBA players saying eligibility rules mean they can enter the 2027 Draft.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Enes Kanter Freedom played 11 seasons in the NBA By Katie Gornall ,  BBC Sport correspondent   and   Katie Falkingham ,  BBC Sport Senior Journalist 
- Published 10 August 2026 
The WNBA is still in the midst of its 2026 season and yet it is next year's Draft for North America's top women's basketball league that is dominating the headlines. 
Why? Because some former men's NBA players have declared they will enter for selection - citing the current eligibility guidelines, or lack of, for transgender women players. 
"I'm officially declaring myself a WNBA prospect," said Enes Kanter Freedom, who played 11 seasons in the NBA. 
It is the latest development in a story ignited by a comment made by Indiana Fever player Sophie Cunningham, who said she wanted to protect young girls "who shouldn't have to go against biological men" in sport. 
Her words have instigated protests - albeit not grand in scale - on both sides of the argument, and once again catapulted the debate around transgender women in sport into the spotlight. 
How did we get here? 
Last month, Cunningham, one of the league's most high-profile players, gave an interview to ESPN , external in which the conversation turned to the topic of "protecting" women's sports. 
The Indiana Fever guard said she had received criticism from people who believed she "hated" transgender people, something she denied. 
She said she wanted to "extend love" to everyone, but added: "I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men." 
She later doubled down on her comments, saying it was "common sense" , external to bar transgender athletes from competing in women's sports. 
Her words quickly moved beyond basketball and into a wider political debate in the United States. 
President Donald Trump expressed his support for Cunningham, while vice-president JD Vance said she was "inspiring". 
Though the 29-year-old later said she is "not a very political person", her remarks have followed her around the country. Competing rallies from critics and supporters were organised at Indiana's games, along with small-scale protests. 
The scale of the debate in the media, online and in politics was striking given no openly transgender woman is due to play, or has ever played, in the WNBA. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Sophie Cunningham is playing in her eighth WNBA season 
What do the rules say? 
The WNBA operates under a collective bargaining agreement (CBA), a deal negotiated between the league and its players association (WNBPA), setting rules on matters including player salary caps, revenue sharing, benefits and overall league operations. 
On player eligibility, the CBA states: "Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA." 
The WNBA has yet to comment publicly on the row since Cunningham's comments but league commissioner Cathy Engelbert reportedly sent a memo to teams last week in which she said the matter would be discussed at an upcoming pre-arranged meeting with team presidents. 
In the memo, seen by the Associated Press , external , Engelbert said the league would "always approach this topic thoughtfully, respectfully, and in alignment with the longstanding values of our league". 
She added: "Our player eligibility rules, unlike the eligibility rules of some other leagues and governing bodies, are collectively bargained. Preserving the integrity of our game and ensuring fair competition will always remain among the league's highest priorities." 
However, the lack of detail in the league's eligibility criteria has been brought to light by Kanter Freedom, who finished his playing career with the Boston Celtics in 2022. 
"If simply declaring who you are is all that's required, then I meet every single requirement necessary to compete in the WNBA," he wrote on Instagram , external . 
Kanter Freedom, who has previously spoken out about human rights violations in China and Turkey, among other issues, added: "I know my presence on the court will stir up strong opinions. I am definitely not here to mock, make fun of, or disrespect any community or personal choices. 
"I'm simply asking that the current rules be applied equally to everyone - the rules that represent the very values many WNBA players and coaches have publicly advocated for." 
A day after Kanter Freedom's 'announcement', Royce White - who made three appearances in the NBA as a player and is now a Republican Senate candidate - said he would also declare for the Draft, adding: "I identify as sometimes identifying as a woman for purpose of basketball." 
Whether the vagueness of the rules are by design to leave it open to transgender women or a sign of an oversight that genuinely needs tightening up is not clear. 
BBC Sport has contacted Cunningham's representatives, the WNBA and WNBPA for comment. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Demonstrators protest before the WNBA matches between Minnesota Lynx and Indiana Fever earlier in August 
What has the reaction been? 
Cunningham's comments have become a flashpoint inside a league which has a long history of player activism on issues including race, gender equality and LGBTQ+ rights. 
The players' association did not mention Cunningham by name when it eventually addressed the debate. 
In a statement the WNBPA denounced "hate abuse and demonisation of the transgender community" and reaffirmed its commitment to "justice, equity, diversity and inclusion". 
It called on fans to report abusive behaviour at games and added that it would continue to have "hard" conversations but it "will not be used as political pawns". 
There is strong feeling on both sides of the argument. Minnesota Lynx head coach and president Cheryl Reeve, who said: "I come from a space of inclusion. 
"The narrative that I think is problematic is to suggest that transgender athletes are the biggest problem in women's sports." 
Reeve wore a "Trans Kids Belong" T-shirt before Minnesota played Indiana earlier this month and was seen speaking to Cunningham on court before the game. 
Cunningham later said the pair had exchanged their perspectives and that the conversation ended with "love and respect". 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Cheryl Reeve wearing a 'Trans Kids Belong' t-shirt 
Golden State Valkyries forward Gabby Williams said she would welcome a transgender athlete "on my team or against my team, any time". 
Last month, the WNBA suspended Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton from attending the team's next five home games after an exchange with two fans, who were sat courtside displaying signs thanking Cunningham for "speaking up for girls". 
Keaton reportedly confronted the teenage fans and admonished them during the game. The Storm have since apologised. 
As for Cunningham, the attention has increasingly become an unwelcome distraction. 
Having defended her original comments, she said recently that she now wanted the conversation to return to what was happening on court. 
"I want to get back to basketball, it's always been about basketball" she said, arguing that the standard of play in the WNBA was being overshadowed by issues away from the game. 
But that may prove difficult, as pressure grows on the league to clarify exactly who is eligible to play. 
What are the rules in other sports? 
In recent years, many governing bodies in sport have amended their rules about the inclusion of transgender athletes at the elite level, moving more towards restrictions. 
Athletics, cycling and aquatics, for example, have implemented outright bans on transgender women taking part in women's events. 
In March, it was announced that the women's category of Olympic sports will be limited to biological females from the LA Olympic Games in 2028. 
The International Olympic Committee (IOC) says eligibility will be determined by a "once-in-a-lifetime" sex test, which would prevent transgender women and those with differences in sexual development (DSD) who have gone through male puberty from competing. 
In the United States, transgender women and girls are banned from competing in women's sports categories in schools, universities and the grassroots level. 
That was part of an executive order - titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" - signed by President Trump last year. 
It does not cover professional sport.

Typhoon Dolphin hits Beijing as city braces for one-third of annual rainfall over 24 hours
Flooding already reported in some districts of Chinese capital and rains are expected to get worse overnight 
Typhoon Dolphin hit China’s capital on Tuesday as the storm caused flooding in parts of Beijing’s Shunyi district. Rains are forecast to intensify overnight. 
Although the storm has been downgraded to a tropical depression, several districts in Beijing activated the highest level of emergency flood responses as the city braced for one-third of its annual rainfall, which is expected over the next 24 hours. 
The ministry of water resources activated a level 4 emergency response and dispatched personnel to badly hit areas in Beijing and the neighbouring port city of Tianjin. 
Chinese state media reported that Beijing ordered more than 250 flood-control teams to be on standby and to prepare flood barriers at subway stations, hospitals and elderly care facilities. 
View image in fullscreen 
Office workers during a heavy rainstorm at rush hour in Beijing earlier this month. Photograph: Kevin Frayer/Getty Images 
From ‌Tuesday evening through to Thursday, most areas in Beijing will experience heavy ‌downpours with a cumulative rainfall of more than 150mm in 24 hours, the city’s meteorological service has forecast. That compares with Beijing’s average annual rainfall of 528mm, the bulk of which normally falls between June and September. Read more 
Four districts on Beijing’s outskirts ​activated level 1 emergency flood responses. In ​the ​mountainous district of ​Mentougou in western Beijing, authorities issued the ​highest ‌level of flood ​emergency alert ​on Tuesday and advised people to stay indoors and avoid travelling to mountainous areas and rivers. 
The strongest typhoon to hit China this year, Dolphin has proved an unusually resilient storm system, travelling nearly 6,000km (3,728 miles) ⁠before making landfall over the weekend, drenching China’s eastern coast and bringing with it a sprawling cloud field. Graphic 
More than a million people were moved to safety across eastern China over the weekend, amid fears torrential rain would cause flooding and landslides. 
Wenzhou, a coastal city in Zhejiang province, said it relocated more than 900,000 people and opened more than 1,500 emergency shelters. In neighbouring Fujian, 98,900 people were moved. 
View image in fullscreen 
Heavy rain and strong winds hit the city of Shanghai on Monday due to Typhoon Dolphin. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images 
In Shanghai, 215,600 people were moved from areas considered at risk by Sunday evening. 
Early on Tuesday Dolphin moved over ​the central Chinese province of Hubei, ​a major auto and hi-tech electronics manufacturing ‌hub and home to more ‌than 58 million people. 
On Tuesday, the national meteorological centre renewed an orange alert for heavy rain, the second-highest warning level, with north-western Hubei expected to receive up to 250mm in a 24-hour period. Hubei authorities have issued a yellow warning for cities including Xiangyang, Huanggang and Suizhou, citing a heightened risk of flooding and landslides. 
Scenic areas across the province have announced temporary closures, ‌including the popular Three Gorges Dam tourist area in Yichang. Of 107 major highway and waterway construction projects under way in the province, 26 projects deemed high-risk have been suspended. 
In neighbouring Henan province, authorities issued a flash-flood alert as the storm continues to ⁠channel moisture northward. 
Japan is also preparing for landslides, flooding and strong winds after the Japan Meteorological Agency said Typhoon Chan-hom could move across Japan’s mainland later on Tuesday.
